# Collections close up: B type motorbus, 1913

## Introduction

The B type bus was the world’s first reliable, mass produced motorbus. Introduced in 1910, it quickly replaced horse buses on London’s streets. 

During the First World War these buses were requisitioned for war service. We have two B type buses in our collection, with this piece focusing on B2737, which was restored to its wartime appearance for the Museum in 2013 to commemorate the centenary of the conflict. We also hold B340, which bears the red livery of the London General Omnibus Company (LGOC).

## Development

Motorbuses became increasingly popular in the 1900s. They were more economical to run and carried more passengers than horse buses. Technology advanced rapidly. Many of the vehicles were short-lived until the largest operator, the London General Omnibus Company (LGOC), introduced the B type bus in 1910. 

 

b/w glass neg, an early motor bus and a horse bus, 1900

The reliable B type combined the best features from a variety of existing models. It was made of interchangeable parts and could be mass produced. Within 18 months the LGOC had replaced its entire fleet of horse buses with B type motorbuses.

 

b/w print, early LGOC B-type bus on tilt test at AEC Walthamstow, 1910 - 1914

Like most early motorbuses, the B type design resembled a horse bus. The driver sat behind the engine in an open cab. On the lower deck passengers sat facing the middle because the body had to fit between the wheels. There was no roof and the wheels had solid tyres. B types remained in service until 1927.

 

B/W photo; B-type buses at Piccadilly Circus by Topical Press, 1914 

## Journeys

Motorbuses could carry more passengers over longer routes than horse buses. Each B type bus had 34 seats, compared to 28 on a horse bus. By 1913 there were 2,500 B type buses carrying 340,000 passengers a year around central London and the suburbs. They also served London’s first night bus routes from 1913, and various leisure outings on Sundays. 

 

B/W print; first night bus outside Piccadilly Underground station, 1913

During the First World War over 1,000 London buses were requisitioned for war service. Many were used as troop carriers, conveying soldiers to and from the front lines. Some were converted into ambulances, lorries or even mobile pigeon lofts. After the war those buses that could be repaired returned to London’s streets.

 

B/W print; LGOC bus converted into pigeon loft, 1914 - 1918

With a third of the LGOC’s fleet on war service, there was a shortage of both buses and staff in London. For the first time women were employed as conductors and mechanics to keep London moving.

 

B/W print; a L.G.O.C. bus conductor and passengers on bus, 1916 - 1919

## Service

Our bus, B2737, started service in January 1914 from Mortlake garage on Route 9, from Barnes to Liverpool Street. It was requisitioned for war service later the same year. After the war it returned to service in London, still in its military livery. It was used as a Traffic Emergency Bus, an austere solution to the post-war bus shortage.

 

B/W print; LGOC B-Type B1167 bus at Mortlake Garage, with driver in summer uniform and conductor, 1910 - 1911

In 1922 the vehicle was sold to the National Omnibus & Transport Company for passenger traffic outside London and from there it passed into private ownership. 

London Transport Museum purchased the body, chassis and engine from a private collector in 2013. With support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund (formerly Heritage Lottery Fund) and London Transport Museum Friends, the vehicle was restored to operational condition. It was converted into a military troop carrier, complete with khaki livery, to commemorate the centenary of the First World War. 

B-type LGOC open top motor bus bonnet No B2737, registration mark LH8186, 1913 

Of the nearly 3,000 B type buses built, only these four now remain. They were united on Covent Garden Piazza outside London Transport Museum for one day on 29 September 2018, with B2737 on the far left. Our other B type, B340, is the second bus on the right.

Four B types at Covent Garden Garden Piazza outside London Transport Museum for one day on 29 September 2018
